event: My manager spent most of our 1:1 discussing things I could improve.
rawInterpretation: My manager is unhappy with my performance.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers often focus on improvement opportunities because strengths may already be meeting expectations.
Discussing improvements does not automatically indicate poor performance.
The conversation may reflect an investment in your growth.
No explicit statement of poor performance was made.
revisedInterpretation: The discussion may have been focused on development rather than criticism.
chosenBehaviour: Ask for both strengths and improvement areas during the next 1:1.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager highlighted several positive contributions and clarified development goals.

event: My manager asked detailed questions about a project update.
rawInterpretation: They suspect I have made mistakes.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers often ask questions to understand status and risks.
Clarifying questions are a normal part of project oversight.
Questions alone do not imply concern or distrust.
No accusation or criticism was expressed.
revisedInterpretation: The questions may simply reflect their responsibility to stay informed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager used the information to prepare for a stakeholder review.

event: My manager took two days to respond to my email.
rawInterpretation: They are avoiding me because they are disappointed.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers often have competing priorities and inbox overload.
Delayed responses happen for many reasons unrelated to performance.
There is no evidence linking the delay to dissatisfaction.
Avoidance is only one of many possible explanations.
revisedInterpretation: The response delay may simply be due to workload.
chosenBehaviour: Send a polite follow-up if necessary.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager replied and apologised for being busy.

event: My manager corrected me during a meeting.
alternateRealityChecks: The correction may have been intended to maintain accuracy.
Everyone occasionally provides incomplete information.
Correcting one statement does not indicate a judgement about competence.
The focus may have been on the topic rather than the person.
revisedInterpretation: The correction may have been about the information, not my capability.
chosenBehaviour: Clarify any misunderstandings and move on.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager later complimented preparation on another topic.

event: A project I led received critical feedback from my manager.
rawInterpretation: The entire project was a failure.
alternateRealityChecks: Projects can succeed while still having improvement areas.
Critical feedback often focuses on specific topics.
One weakness does not invalidate the whole project.
Successful projects regularly undergo review and critique.
revisedInterpretation: The project may still have delivered value despite the feedback.
chosenBehaviour: Capture lessons learned and improvement actions.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Stakeholders confirmed satisfaction with overall project outcomes.

event: My manager praised a colleague during team updates but did not mention my work.
alternateRealityChecks: Recognition can be influenced by timing and visibility.
Someone else's praise does not imply others are unvalued.
Managers cannot mention every contribution every time.
One meeting does not establish a pattern.
revisedInterpretation: The lack of recognition in one meeting does not define how my work is viewed.
chosenBehaviour: Continue delivering impact and discuss visibility if needed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager referenced several of my contributions during planning discussions.

event: My manager asked me to revise a document before sharing it.
alternateRealityChecks: Documents often go through multiple review cycles.
Requested revisions can improve clarity rather than fix problems.
Managers may have different expectations for the audience.
Needing edits does not mean the work is poor.
revisedInterpretation: The document may have been good but needed refinement.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The document was approved and shared widely.

event: My manager asked if I needed help on a challenging task.
rawInterpretation: They think I cannot handle the task.
alternateRealityChecks: Offering support is a normal leadership behaviour.
Managers help reduce risks on important work.
The question may reflect care rather than doubt.
There is no evidence of a negative judgement.
revisedInterpretation: The offer may have been intended to support success.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Additional support accelerated completion of the task.

event: My manager asked about career goals unexpectedly.
rawInterpretation: They may be planning changes to my role.
alternateRealityChecks: Career discussions are common development activities.
Managers often explore aspirations during planning cycles.
No information about role changes was provided.
There may be positive reasons behind the discussion.
revisedInterpretation: The discussion likely relates to development rather than a hidden concern.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager suggested growth opportunities aligned with my interests.

event: My manager requested more frequent status updates.
alternateRealityChecks: Projects sometimes require increased visibility.
Stakeholder pressure may require more reporting.
The request may be process-related rather than personal.
Trust cannot be evaluated from this request alone.
revisedInterpretation: The additional updates may be driven by project needs.
chosenBehaviour: Provide updates and seek context if needed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager explained leadership requested greater transparency.

event: My manager did not immediately support my proposal.
rawInterpretation: They do not believe in my ideas.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers often evaluate proposals from multiple perspectives.
Questions can indicate engagement rather than rejection.
The timing may not be right.
One proposal does not represent all future ideas.
revisedInterpretation: The proposal may simply require further validation.
chosenBehaviour: Gather evidence and strengthen the proposal.

event: My manager cancelled our check-in meeting.
rawInterpretation: I am no longer important to them.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers frequently reprioritise schedules.
A cancelled meeting does not indicate reduced support.
Many external factors may affect availability.
No evidence suggests a change in relationship.
revisedInterpretation: The cancellation is more likely scheduling related.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The meeting was rescheduled and held normally.

event: My manager asked me to present to leadership.
rawInterpretation: I am being tested and will fail.
alternateRealityChecks: High-visibility opportunities are often given to trusted contributors.
Presenting does not imply a hidden test.
The invitation may reflect confidence in your work.
Failure is not the most likely outcome.
revisedInterpretation: This may be an opportunity rather than a threat.

event: My manager compared my approach to another employee's approach.
rawInterpretation: I am being measured and found lacking.
alternateRealityChecks: Comparisons can be used to share ideas and approaches.
Different methods may suit different situations.
The comparison may not have been evaluative.
No direct criticism was expressed.
revisedInterpretation: The comparison may have been intended as a learning opportunity.
chosenBehaviour: Explore what can be learned from the example.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The discussion helped improve future planning.

event: My manager said my work could have a greater impact with some changes.
rawInterpretation: My current work has little value.
alternateRealityChecks: Greater impact implies existing value already exists.
Improvement suggestions do not negate contributions.
Feedback can build upon success.
The statement acknowledges potential rather than failure.
revisedInterpretation: My work is valuable and can become even more effective.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The revised work received strong stakeholder feedback.
